title: Chinese state media persuades a global audience that the “China model” is superior: Evidence from a 19-country experiment

reviewed_pages.boundary_confirmation: All 18 PDF pages are the published main article. PDF page 1 starts at printed p. 1029 and PDF page 18 ends at p. 1046; no appendix is embedded.

source_scope: Only the supplied published main article (PDF pp. 1–18 / printed pp. 1029–1046), including main-text tables, figures, notes, and footnotes. Online appendices, replication files, preregistration, and external sources were excluded; pointers to them received no evidentiary credit.

experiments.name: 19-country state-media video survey experiment
experiments.classification_rationale: A new sample of Lucid respondents was randomly assigned within country to four video conditions and analyzed for post-exposure outcomes. Nested random clip selection is part of this same treatment design, not a separate sample or separately reported experiment.

design_map.label: Target population
design_map.value: A 'global audience' operationalized as Lucid respondents in 19 named countries across six continents; not a random population draw.

evidence.anchor: recruited respondents through the survey firm Lucid in the following 19 countries

findings: Prose, figure content, figure notes, and footnotes were treated as coequal main-article evidence.
Figure 6 arm distributions received credit as raw group quantities even though they were not repeated in prose.
Figures 7–9 received credit for labeled point estimates, but not for uncertainty because the visible bars were not identified by type, level, or construction in their notes or prose.
Figure 5 arm counts were transcribed and arithmetically checked, revealing that 1,662+1,565+1,531+1,558=6,316, inconsistent with the displayed/text total 6,276.
Appendix pointers were recorded only as evidence that information was absent from the permitted source, never as evidence that it was reported.

direct_comparison.scope: One paper and one scored experiment were supplied; a cross-paper winner or ranking is therefore not defined.
direct_comparison.summary: The experiment is strongest on explicit estimand, analysis unit, multiplicity/status, and inferential scope. Reconstructability is limited by missing exact stimuli, inconsistent participant counts, incomplete model coding/specification, missing analysis Ns, and undefined graphical uncertainty.

consistency_audit.statement: Prose, figures, tables, table notes, and footnotes were given equal evidentiary status. Figure 1 supplied the displayed power-sharing script and raw response codes; Figures 4–5 supplied group means and intervals; Tables 4–5 and their notes supplied observations, fixed effects, clustering, bootstrap, p-values, coefficients, and column outcomes. No score was reduced merely because evidence appeared in a display. Conversely, estimator and confidence-interval details were not inferred from conventional table appearance, and SI pointers were not credited as reporting.

title: How Markets Shape Values and Political Preferences: A Field Experiment

reviewed_pages.boundary_note: PDF pages 1–19 contain the article through references; PDF page 20 (printed 492) contains only a Supporting Information availability/index notice. No appendix content is embedded.

source_scope: Only the supplied published main article, including main-text tables, figures, notes, and footnotes. Online supporting information, verification materials, preregistrations, registries, code, replication files, and external methods references were not consulted or credited.

experiments.name: Six-week market-engagement field experiment and original-assignment follow-up
experiments.classification_rationale: A new sample of 2,703 participants was block-randomized once to control or six treatment/subtreatment destinations. Weekly investment exposure, post-treatment outcomes, mechanism outcomes, and the July 2017 follow-up all use that original assignment and therefore form one primary experiment.

consistency_audit.statement: Prose, equations, tables, table notes, figures, figure notes, and footnotes were given equal evidentiary status. Table 1 supplied payoff cells; Table 2 supplied group quantities; Tables 3–4 and their notes supplied model outputs; footnotes 3–4 supplied weighting and alternative-specification details. No score was reduced merely because evidence appeared in a display, and no appendix pointer was credited as reporting omitted information.

direct_comparison.scope: One-paper independent assessment; cross-paper synthesis is deferred. Within this paper, E1 is the clearest statistically because its treatment table and AMCE model are in the main text. E3 and E4 report focal figures but omit parts of the computational/inference specification. E2 is least transparent because its design and numerical analysis are relegated to excluded supporting information.

findings: Table 1 received the same evidentiary weight as prose for exact E1 vignette wording and factor levels.
Figure 1 and its note received credit for analysis N, outcome scale, estimates, confidence intervals, and reference categories.
Figure 2 and its note received credit for N, contrasts, reference levels, estimates, and intervals, but not for unreported regression terms or CI construction.
Figure 3 and Table 2 notes received credit for outcomes, adjustments, estimates, intervals, mediation equations, and 1,000 simulations.
Pointers to SI/appendices were treated only as evidence that details were absent from the main article.

execution_record.original_model_output: This structured review and report are the original session output; no post-hoc correction applied.

title: Changing In-Group Boundaries: The Effect of Immigration on Race Relations in the United States

reviewed_pages.boundary_note: The supplied PDF contains the complete 17-page published main article. Printed page 968 begins the title/abstract and printed page 984 ends the references; no appendix pages are embedded. Experimental scoring used the full article, with the experiment account on PDF pages 11–13 (printed 978–980) reviewed textually and Figure 4 on PDF page 12 inspected visually.

source_scope: Published main article only: all PDF pages 1–17, including main-text tables, figures, notes, and footnotes. Online Appendix, replication materials, and all external sources were excluded; pointers to them received no evidentiary credit.

experiments.name: Lucid Hispanic-population salience prime

direct_comparison.scope: Single-paper independent assessment; cross-paper synthesis is deferred.
direct_comparison.finding: Within this paper, Figure 4 makes the experimental contrast, plotted effects, and confidence levels visible, but the supporting survey experiment is substantially less reconstructable than a fully specified analysis because allocation, outcome coding, estimator, controls, dependence adjustment, analytic Ns, and missing-data rules are omitted from the main article.

consistency_audit.statement: Prose, figures, figure notes, tables, table notes, and footnotes were given equal evidentiary status. Figure 4 and its note earned credit for plotted coefficients, control means, specifications labeled with/without controls, and 90%/95% intervals. The note's pointer to Online Appendix Section F and footnote 12's pointer to replication materials did not supply omitted information. No score was reduced merely because evidence appeared graphically rather than in prose.

direct_comparison.scope: Single-paper independent assessment; comparison is across its separately scored experiments, not across papers.
direct_comparison.summary: Study 1 reports richer direct and mediation estimates (means, mean differences, SEs, OLS paths, indirect-effect SEs and interval limits) than Study 2, which reports condition means, omnibus F tests, eta squared and p values without contrast uncertainty. All five experiments share major gaps in allocation probabilities, flow, exact stimuli, missingness, multiplicity, and analysis-status reporting.

Tables 1–4 and Figures 1–2 earned credit where they supplied coding, means, effects, SEs, intervals, covariates, or model labels. consistency_audit.statement: Prose, equations, main-text tables, figures, table notes, figure notes, and footnotes were given equal evidentiary status. Tables 5 and 6 earned credit for their equations, OLS labels, fixed-effect changes, covariate names, counts, estimates, pooled means/SDs, and t statistics. They did not earn credit for unstated standard-error/dependence procedures, absent SEs/CIs, or definitions deferred to online appendices. Appendix pointers were never treated as supplying omitted content.
findings: Table 5 confirms negative GovernmentTies coefficients of −0.114 and −0.079 with t statistics, not standard errors.

consistency_audit.statement: Prose, equations, tables, table notes, figures, figure notes and footnotes in the main article received equal evidentiary status. Tables 3–5 earned credit for outcomes, coding, samples, estimates, control means and uncertainty. No item was reduced merely because evidence appeared in a display. Conversely, names such as double-post-lasso, randomization inference, or bootstrap did not earn reconstructability credit where implementation details were absent. Appendix pointers were recorded only as evidence of absence and never as evidence that omitted content was reported.

consistency_audit.statement: Prose, figures, Table 1, and the Table 1 note received equal evidentiary status. Credit for arm Ns, raw rates, reference category, odds ratios, and thresholded P values came directly from Table 1 and its note. No credit was withheld merely because evidence appeared in a display. Appendix pointers supplied no evidence. A numerical discrepancy was preserved: pooled not-interested OR is 0.44 in Table 1 but 0.40 in the prose; neither was silently preferred.
findings: Table 1 and its note support criteria 6–10 and 14–17 where their contents are sufficient.
The page-3 prose supports pooled chi-square statistics and 95% confidence intervals.
The SI Appendix pointers on pages 1–3 were excluded as instructed.
The pooled not-interested OR inconsistency (0.44 table; 0.40 prose) is recorded in the design map and report.

execution_record.submission_text:
Act as an independent reviewer of experimental reporting. Evaluate whether a competent applied researcher can reconstruct each experiment and its statistical analysis using only the published main article.

Do not evaluate novelty, substantive importance, journal prestige, or whether you agree with the conclusions. Do not seek a predetermined winner. Apply exactly the same evidentiary standard to every paper.

## Papers

Review the following published main articles:

AJPS053: attached article.pdf. DOI: 10.1111/ajps.12758.

## Source restriction

Use only the published main article, including its main-text tables, figures, table notes, figure notes, and footnotes.

Do not consult online appendices, supplementary information, preregistrations, registries, replication files, code, or external methodological references. A reference to excluded material does not supply the omitted information.

Use the 20 core criteria below to define the assessment. If an additional reporting checklist is supplied, use it only to define its scoring items and components; it is not evidence about the papers. If no additional checklist is supplied, omit the separate checklist assessment.

Do not search for or substitute any external reporting standard or checklist. Online access is permitted only to obtain the identified published main articles. All paper-specific evidence must come from those main articles.

## Unit of evaluation

First identify every distinct randomized experiment.

Classify each as:

1. Primary experiment
2. Supporting experiment with a formal statistical analysis
3. Brief diagnostic randomization or robustness check
4. Pilot with no reported outcome
5. Observational analysis

Score categories 1–3 separately. List categories 4–5 without scoring them as experiments.

Do not combine all randomizations into a single article-level score. Report primary, supporting, and diagnostic experiments separately.

A follow-up using the original randomized assignment belongs to the original experiment. A new randomized sample or manipulation is a separate experiment.

Classify each experiment using all labels supported by the design described in the main article: completely randomized experiment, cluster-randomized experiment, factorial experiment, conjoint experiment, survey experiment, or list experiment. If the article provides too little information to classify it, mark it Unclear.

## Binary scoring

Use:

- **1 = fully meets the reporting standard**
- **0 = does not fully meet the reporting standard**
- **N/A = logically inapplicable**

Do not award partial credit. If a material component required by a criterion is missing, score the entire criterion 0.

Use N/A only when the concept cannot apply to the design. Failure to report information is 0, not N/A.

## Evidence rule

A regression equation is not required when a regression table and its notes jointly make the analysis completely unambiguous.

A regression table may earn full credit when it clearly identifies:

- Outcome
- Treatment or experimental contrast
- Treatment and control coding
- Omitted or reference category
- Analysis unit
- Estimator
- Covariates or fixed effects in each specification
- Standard-error procedure
- Clustering or other dependence adjustment
- Analysis sample size
- Effect estimate
- Uncertainty measure
- Correspondence between the table column and the result discussed in the text

Do not reduce a score merely because information appears in a table rather than prose.

Conversely, merely naming an estimator—such as OLS, AMCE, marginal means, conditional AMCE, or bootstrap—does not earn credit when the reader cannot reconstruct how it was implemented.

## Design map

Before scoring, create the following map for every scored experiment:

- Target population
- Eligibility criteria
- Recruitment procedure
- Field dates and setting
- Number recruited and analyzed
- Experimental arms or randomized attributes
- Unit of randomization
- Allocation probabilities and restrictions
- Exact treatment and comparator
- Outcome definitions and timing
- Estimand
- Estimator or statistical model
- Analysis unit
- Variable coding and reference categories
- Covariates and fixed effects
- Standard-error and inference procedure
- Handling of clustering or repeated observations
- Missing-data and attrition rules
- Effect estimates and uncertainty

Cite the page, table, figure, or footnote supporting every entry. Write “NR” when an element is not reported. Do not infer standard practice.

## Core reporting criteria

Score every experiment on the following criteria.

### Experimental design

1. **Population and recruitment:** Target population, eligibility, recruitment, and major exclusions are fully reported.
2. **Experimental conditions:** Treatment and comparator, or all randomized attributes and levels, are reported precisely enough to reproduce.
3. **Randomization**: The unit of random assignment, whether assignment was stratified, and any restrictions on treatment assignment probabilities are clear. Details specified by the definition of the named design count unless the paper describes a conflicting procedure.
4. **Outcome measurement:** Outcomes, coding, timing, and primary or secondary status are fully reported.
5. **Participant flow:** Numbers recruited, randomized, exposed, followed, and analyzed are reported as applicable.

### Statistical methods

6. **Estimand:** The causal or descriptive quantity being estimated is explicitly defined, whether presented as an estimand, a target parameter, a parameter of interest, or a well-defined causal effect.
7. **Estimator/model:** The statistical operation used to estimate the estimand is reconstructable from the text, table, or table notes.
8. **Analysis unit:** The reader can determine whether observations are participants, profiles, choices, sessions, or another unit.
9. **Coding and reference categories:** Treatment coding, outcome coding, omitted categories, and reference levels are explicit.
10. **Specification:** Covariates, fixed effects, weights, transformations, and column-to-column specification changes are explicit.
11. **Dependence and inference:** Standard errors, clustering, repeated-observation dependence, bootstrap or permutation procedures, and confidence-interval construction are explicit.
12. **Missingness and attrition:** Inclusion rules, missing outcomes, exclusions, attrition, and corresponding adjustments are explicit.
13. **Multiplicity and analysis status:** Multiple-testing procedures and prespecified versus exploratory analyses are distinguished.

### Results

14. **Analysis sample:** The number of observations used in each focal analysis is reported.
15. **Group quantities:** Relevant control means, treatment means, marginal means, or other raw quantities are reported.
16. **Effect and uncertainty:** Effect estimates and standard errors or confidence intervals are reported.
17. **Model-to-result traceability:** Each focal numerical result can be connected directly to a particular outcome, contrast, specification, sample, and inference procedure.
18. **Robustness analyses:** Alternative specifications and sensitivity analyses are explained sufficiently to understand what changed.

### Validity assessment

19. **Internal-validity threats:** Attrition, noncompliance, spillovers, demand effects, measurement problems, and other relevant threats are discussed.
20. **Inferential scope:** The paper distinguishes the randomized contrast from broader claims about mechanisms, populations, and settings.

## Component-level scoring

Treat each criterion as a compound item when it contains multiple required components.

Display the score and evidence for every component. Give the overall criterion a score of 1 only when every applicable component scores 1. Do not count component scores separately in the criterion totals.

For example:

- Criterion 1 components: target population, eligibility, recruitment, major exclusions
- Criterion 3 components: unit of random assignment, whether assignment was stratified, restrictions on treatment assignment probabilities
- Criterion 4 components: outcome definition, coding, timing, primary/secondary status
- Criterion 11 components: standard errors, clustering, repeated-observation handling, resampling procedures, confidence-interval construction
- Criterion 20 components: randomized contrast, mechanism scope, population scope, setting scope

Explain every component-level N/A judgment.

## Design-specific standards

### Ordinary treatment-control experiments

Award full statistical-model credit when the main-text regression table and notes jointly identify the outcome, treatment indicator, omitted control condition, analysis unit, adjustments, inference method, sample size, estimate, and uncertainty.

Do not require a redundant mathematical equation.

### List experiments

Require:

- Control list
- Treatment list
- Sensitive item
- Randomization mechanism
- Difference-in-means estimator
- Analysis unit
- Variance or confidence-interval procedure
- Sample size
- Numerical estimate

### Conjoint experiments

Award full credit only when the main article reports:

- Number of tasks and profiles per respondent
- Attribute levels and assignment probabilities
- Restrictions on profile construction
- Outcome coding
- Exact estimand
- Estimating model or computational procedure
- Analysis unit
- Reference categories
- Treatment of paired profiles and repeated observations
- Respondent-level clustering or another justified dependence adjustment
- Analysis sample size
- Direct mapping from the model to every focal AMCE, marginal mean, or related figure

The statement “we estimate AMCEs,” a citation to a standard conjoint article, or a pointer to an appendix is insufficient.

### Brief diagnostic randomizations

Score these separately. Do not average them with primary or formally analyzed experiments.

If only two percentages are reported without an explicit contrast, uncertainty calculation, or arm-specific sample sizes, score the missing statistical criteria 0.

## Additional checklist assessment

Complete this section only if an additional reporting checklist is supplied. Do not obtain one independently.

After completing the reconstructability assessment, provide a separate table for the supplied checklist.

For compound checklist items, divide the item into its required components. Give the item a score of 1 only if every applicable component is fully reported; otherwise score it 0.

Keep article-level items—such as title, funding, conflicts, registration, and data access—separate from experiment-level methods and results.

Do not use the overall checklist total as a measure of statistical-model clarity.

Report separately:

1. Overall completeness under the supplied checklist
2. Experimental-design reporting
3. Statistical-method transparency
4. Results transparency
5. Internal-validity discussion

## Required output

Produce:

1. An experiment inventory with one row per entry and separate **Study category** and **Experiment design** columns. List all design labels supported by the main article in full. Use **Unclear** if no design label can be determined and **N/A** for observational analyses.
2. A design map for every scored experiment
3. A binary criterion-by-experiment table
4. Separate totals for experimental design, statistical methods, results, and validity
5. A separate table for any additional supplied checklist
6. A concise explanation of every 0, identifying the exact missing information
7. A direct comparison of the papers’ statistical transparency
8. A consistency audit confirming that tables and table notes received the same evidentiary status as prose

Do not produce a combined article-level score that averages primary, supporting, and diagnostic experiments.

## HTML presentation and scoring evidence

Save the output as a polished, self-contained HTML file that opens offline.

The HTML must include:

- Embedded styling
- Clear navigation
- Desktop, mobile, and print-friendly layouts
- Full paper titles
- Experiment inventory with separate Study category and Experiment design columns, with all supported design labels shown in full
- Source-scope statement
- A prominent notice that AI-generated judgments await human review
- Experiment-level category subtotals
- A direct comparison table
- A consistency audit
- Downloadable scored JSON embedded in the HTML

For every core criterion and supplied checklist item, show:

- Identifier
- Complete wording
- Overall score
- Concise rationale
- Required components
- Component-level scores
- Supporting evidence or exact absence explanation

For each evidentiary record, provide:

- A concise verbatim anchor, subject to applicable quotation limits
- A page-specific paraphrase explaining the relevant evidence
- One-based PDF page number
- Printed page number, where available
- Table, figure, section, note, or footnote locator

Make every score in the criterion matrix link to its evidence details.

For missing information:

- State exactly what is absent
- Identify the main-article pages and displays reviewed
- Do not invent a quotation to prove an absence
- Do not treat an appendix pointer as evidence that the missing information was reported

For N/A judgments:

- Explain why the concept cannot logically apply
- Exclude the item from the denominator

Show numerators, applicable-item denominators, and N/A counts for every subtotal.

Keep core scores, supplied-checklist scores, article-level items, and experiment-level items clearly separated. Do not double-count component scores in item totals.

The downloadable JSON and visible HTML tables must be generated from the same scored records.

## Final constraints

Do not give credit for customary practice, inferred implementation, or information available only outside the main article.

Do give full credit when the main-text table and its notes together make an analysis completely reconstructable.

Apply the same standard to every paper and report the resulting differences without seeking a predetermined winner.

experiments.name: Birmingham partisan telephone campaign and household-spillover experiment
experiments.classification_rationale: This is the article's sole newly analyzed randomized assignment. One person per two-voter household was blocked by party preference and assigned to high-intensity call, low-intensity call, or no-contact control. Direct ITT, household-spillover, conditional logistic, and CACE analyses all reuse this assignment and are therefore part of one experiment.
experiments.design_label_note: This is an ordinary three-arm randomized treatment-control experiment implemented within three strata. The person, not the household as a cluster, is described as the assignment unit; household spillover measurement does not by itself make the design cluster-randomized. It is not factorial, conjoint, survey, or list.

rows.summary: Strong main-text reporting of the arms, administrative turnout, raw ITTs, effect uncertainty, and limitations; insufficient main-text detail for exact scripts, assignment probabilities, randomization-inference implementation, several logistic/CACE computations, complete flow, coding, multiplicity, and figure-specific Ns.

direct_comparison.note: A direct pairwise comparison is impossible because this session contains one paper. The row preserves experiment-level results for later cross-paper synthesis without creating an article-level average.

consistency_audit.statement: Prose, main-text tables, figures, table/figure notes, and footnotes were treated as equal evidence. Table 1 received credit for group rates, contrasts, intervals, N, weighting notice, and randomization-inference label; Table 2 received credit for coefficients, reference group, covariate changes, N, and parenthetical uncertainty. Credit was withheld only where those displays and notes still omitted implementation details. Pointers to supporting information were recorded as absence evidence and did not supply omitted content.

Table 1 was visually inspected for row/column alignment, intervals, Ns, and note text.
Figures 3–5 and Table 2 were visually inspected for confidence-interval notes, reference groups, model columns, and N.

title: Can Party Elites Shape the Rank and File? Evidence from a Recruitment Campaign in India

reviewed_pages.boundary_note: All 20 PDF pages are the published main article. PDF pp. 19–20 are references. No appendix or supplementary pages are embedded.

source_scope: Published main article only: article.pdf, including main-text prose, tables, figures, notes and footnotes. Supplementary material, appendices, preregistration, data and replication files were excluded even when cited.

experiments.name: AAP Jharkhand pamphlet recruitment experiment
experiments.classification_rationale: The article's central causal study cross-randomizes gender portrayal at assembly level and benefit messages at vice-president level; onboarding and three-year retention use the original assignment.

findings: Main-text Tables 1–4 and their notes were treated as evidence on the same basis as prose.
Figure notes earned credit for identifying outcomes, grouping, and 95% confidence intervals; unlabeled implementation details were not inferred from graphics.
Table 2 received credit for the content it displays, but its pointer to appendix pages 21–25 did not supply absent exact SSI/MTurk wording.
Footnotes received full evidentiary status; appendix pointers in footnotes did not count as reporting the omitted model details.
Visible PDF pages 7–16 were checked against rendered page images for figure/table layout and column order.

direct_comparison.scope: Within-paper experiment comparison only; this independent session contains one paper and therefore cannot make an inter-paper ranking.
direct_comparison.summary: Study 1 and Study 2 use the same transparent OLS equation and Table 2 note, so estimator, analysis unit, subgroup sample size, effect estimates, robust standard errors, and model-to-result mapping are similarly clear. Both omit exact stimuli, allocation details, exact outcome coding, flow/missingness rules, raw arm means, multiplicity status, and mechanism-scope boundaries. Study 2 has an additional unexplained difference between 156 recruited and 154 analyzed participants.

consistency_audit.statement: Main-text tables, figures, notes, equations, prose, and footnotes were given equal evidentiary status. Table 2 and its note earned credit for treatment coding, estimator linkage, subgroup sample sizes, coefficients, robust standard errors, and two-tailed tests. experiments.name: Google Consumer Surveys issue-selection pilots
experiments.classification_rationale: Small statewide pilot surveys selected four relatively unpopular positions per legislator; no pilot outcome, sample, or randomization analysis is reported.

direct_comparison.scope: Within-paper comparison only; cross-paper synthesis is deferred.
direct_comparison.finding: Study 1 and Study 2 have similar statistical transparency: regression tables identify OLS specifications, analysis units, samples, coefficients and SEs. Study 2 provides a clearer three-arm comparator and a main-text variance diagnostic, but omits randomized/recruited totals and arm probabilities and contains a 1,047-voter versus 1,140-cluster inconsistency. Both omit complete treatment materials, binary approval cutpoints, CI construction, multiplicity handling, raw group means, and full missing-data rules.

consistency_audit.statement: Prose, tables, table notes, and footnotes were given equal evidentiary status. Tables 3–8 earned credit where their headings, rows and notes jointly identified outcomes, contrasts, estimators, covariates, units, sample sizes, estimates and SE procedures. Appendix pointers received no credit. The Study 2 prose/Table 7 respondent-count conflict was retained rather than harmonized.

findings.detail: Table and note evidence supported criteria 7, 8, 10, 14, 16 and 17 without requiring redundant prose.
Pointers to Supplementary Appendices A–D did not supply omitted letter texts, questionnaires, balance checks, or robustness results.
PDF p. 8 says 2,528 observations from 1,047 voters; Table 7 on PDF p. 9 reports 2,528 observations and 1,140 respondent clusters.

execution_record.token_usage_note: Token usage was not exposed to the session runtime.

direct_comparison.scope_note: This independent session contains one paper, so no between-paper ranking is possible. Within the article, all three primary country experiments have the same reporting structure and therefore the same core subtotal pattern. The three order diagnostics are much less transparent because only their existence and purpose are reported.

rows.comparison: Identical method reporting: estimands and respondent analysis unit are clear; plotted effects/95% CIs are available; allocation details, exact outcome coding, focal Ns, raw means, variance/CI construction, missingness, and multiplicity are absent.
Only randomization purpose is disclosed. Arms, unit, allocation, estimator, sample sizes, effects, and uncertainty are not reported.

consistency_audit.statement: Prose, figure panels, figure labels, footnotes, and notes were given equal evidentiary status. Figures 1–5 earned effect-and-uncertainty credit because they visibly plot point estimates and 95% confidence intervals. Footnotes earned credit where they supplied design or transformation facts. Conversely, SI/appendix pointers did not earn credit for omitted specifications or results.

checks.treatment: Counted as evidence for outcomes, contrasts, point estimates, and 95% confidence intervals.
Counted equally with prose (e.g., 0–1 rescaling, extra government arm, randomized item order, weights sensitivity).
No main-text regression table is present; no table-note evidence was available to count or discount.
Recorded as absence locations, never as evidence that omitted details were reported.

title: Behavioral nudges prevent loan delinquencies at scale: A 13-million-person field experiment
source_scope: Published main article only: PDF pages 1–8, including main-text prose, Figures 1–2 and their notes, Tables 1–3 and their notes, and footnotes. Supporting information, preregistrations, external references, code, and online materials were excluded.
main_article_boundary: Eight PDF pages, each labeled 1 of 8 through 8 of 8. Page 8 contains affiliations, acknowledgments, and references; no supplementary pages are embedded.

experiments.name: Six-arm federal student-loan email field experiment
experiments.classification_rationale: The article presents one new randomized sample with six borrower-level email arms and formal analyses. The four reminder arms cross percentage/dollar framing with repeated-two/sequential-one-action messaging, an embedded 2×2 factorial. All contrasts use the same randomized cohort and therefore remain one experiment.

title: Conditional cooperation and confusion in public-goods experiments

source_scope: Published main article only, including main-text Tables 1, Figures 1–3, notes, footnote, and Methods. SI Appendix, SI Methods, SI Results, SI Discussion, Tables S1–S6, Figures S1–S3, external references, registrations, code, and data were excluded and were not treated as evidence.

title: The Effects of Exposure to Better Neighborhoods on Children: New Evidence from the Moving to Opportunity Experiment
source_scope: Only the supplied published main article PDF was used. PDF pages 1–48 correspond to printed pages 855–902. The article starts on PDF page 1 and ends with references on PDF page 48. Online appendices, linked additional materials, cited reports, replication files, and external standards were excluded as evidence.

experiments.name: Moving to Opportunity randomized housing-voucher experiment and linked long-term follow-up
experiments.classification_rationale: The article's central causal evidence uses the original MTO family-level random assignment. Child, adult, first-stage, subgroup, tax, and later follow-up analyses reuse that assignment and therefore belong to one experiment. The article reports no new participant randomization; simulated placebo reassignments are an inference procedure, not a separate experiment.

consistency_audit.statement: Main-text tables, figures, notes, footnotes, and prose received equal evidentiary status. Full credit was awarded where equations plus table notes made analyses reconstructable (notably criteria 6–9, 15–17). Scores were not reduced merely because evidence appeared in a display. Appendix pointers were not treated as evidence, and omitted details behind those pointers caused failures where material.
checks: Table 3 notes were used to establish outcomes, estimators, units, covariates, clustered SEs, Ns, estimates, and uncertainty.
Table 2 notes were used for first-stage and TOT specifications and sample definitions.
Figure notes were used for model mapping, but missing per-bin sample sizes were not inferred.
Footnotes were credited for linkage, measurement, and identifying-assumption details.
Online appendix references supplied no omitted covariate lists, results, or methods.

direct_comparison.interpretation: Single-paper session: no cross-paper ranking is possible. The experiment is strongest on estimand/model/result traceability and weakest on exact allocation/weight reconstruction, full participant flow, and analysis-status reporting.

inventory_notes: No pilots without outcomes, diagnostic randomizations, supporting randomized experiments, or observational analyses were identified. Descriptive comparisons to the original HLCS sample are contextual participant-flow checks, not a distinct analysis entered in the inventory.

direct_comparison.statement: Only P113 was supplied in this session, so no cross-paper ranking is possible. Within P113, Table 1 is materially more transparent than the prose-only transfer analyses: the table identifies outcomes, estimates, robust SEs, control means, N, and adjustments, whereas secondary transfer results omit N, model details, and uncertainty.

findings: Table 1 and its note received the same evidentiary status as prose.
Table 1 earned credit for estimator, covariates/fixed effects, robust SEs, sample sizes, control means, effects, uncertainty, and column/sample mapping.
No score was reduced merely because information appeared in a table.
Supplementary-material pointers were recorded as pointers only and did not supply omitted details.

Tables 2–3 earned credit for the outcome reference, covariates, standard errors as displayed, sample sizes, estimates, and uncertainty; they did not earn credit for the unreported standard-error type or missing covariate scales. execution_record.submission:
Act as an independent reviewer of experimental reporting. Evaluate whether a competent applied researcher can reconstruct each experiment and its statistical analysis using only the published main article.

Do not evaluate novelty, substantive importance, journal prestige, or whether you agree with the conclusions. Do not seek a predetermined winner. Apply exactly the same evidentiary standard to every paper.

## Papers

Review the following published main articles:

AJPS016: attached article.pdf. DOI: 10.1111/ajps.12582.

## Source restriction

Use only the published main article, including its main-text tables, figures, table notes, figure notes, and footnotes.

Do not consult online appendices, supplementary information, preregistrations, registries, replication files, code, or external methodological references. A reference to excluded material does not supply the omitted information.

Use the 20 core criteria below to define the assessment. If an additional reporting checklist is supplied, use it only to define its scoring items and components; it is not evidence about the papers. If no additional checklist is supplied, omit the separate checklist assessment.

Do not search for or substitute any external reporting standard or checklist. Online access is permitted only to obtain the identified published main articles. All paper-specific evidence must come from those main articles.

## Unit of evaluation

First identify every distinct randomized experiment.

Classify each as:

1. Primary experiment
2. Supporting experiment with a formal statistical analysis
3. Brief diagnostic randomization or robustness check
4. Pilot with no reported outcome
5. Observational analysis

Score categories 1–3 separately. List categories 4–5 without scoring them as experiments.

Do not combine all randomizations into a single article-level score. Report primary, supporting, and diagnostic experiments separately.

A follow-up using the original randomized assignment belongs to the original experiment. A new randomized sample or manipulation is a separate experiment.

Classify each experiment using all labels supported by the design described in the main article: completely randomized experiment, cluster-randomized experiment, factorial experiment, conjoint experiment, survey experiment, or list experiment. If the article provides too little information to classify it, mark it Unclear.

## Binary scoring

Use:

- **1 = fully meets the reporting standard**
- **0 = does not fully meet the reporting standard**
- **N/A = logically inapplicable**

Do not award partial credit. If a material component required by a criterion is missing, score the entire criterion 0.

Use N/A only when the concept cannot apply to the design. Failure to report information is 0, not N/A.

## Evidence rule

A regression equation is not required when a regression table and its notes jointly make the analysis completely unambiguous.

A regression table may earn full credit when it clearly identifies:

- Outcome
- Treatment or experimental contrast
- Treatment and control coding
- Omitted or reference category
- Analysis unit
- Estimator
- Covariates or fixed effects in each specification
- Standard-error procedure
- Clustering or other dependence adjustment
- Analysis sample size
- Effect estimate
- Uncertainty measure
- Correspondence between the table column and the result discussed in the text

Do not reduce a score merely because information appears in a table rather than prose.

Conversely, merely naming an estimator—such as OLS, AMCE, marginal means, conditional AMCE, or bootstrap—does not earn credit when the reader cannot reconstruct how it was implemented.

## Design map

Before scoring, create the following map for every scored experiment:

- Target population
- Eligibility criteria
- Recruitment procedure
- Field dates and setting
- Number recruited and analyzed
- Experimental arms or randomized attributes
- Unit of randomization
- Allocation probabilities and restrictions
- Exact treatment and comparator
- Outcome definitions and timing
- Estimand
- Estimator or statistical model
- Analysis unit
- Variable coding and reference categories
- Covariates and fixed effects
- Standard-error and inference procedure
- Handling of clustering or repeated observations
- Missing-data and attrition rules
- Effect estimates and uncertainty

Cite the page, table, figure, or footnote supporting every entry. Write “NR” when an element is not reported. Do not infer standard practice.

## Core reporting criteria

Score every experiment on the following criteria.

### Experimental design

1. **Population and recruitment:** Target population, eligibility, recruitment, and major exclusions are fully reported.
2. **Experimental conditions:** Treatment and comparator, or all randomized attributes and levels, are reported precisely enough to reproduce.
3. **Randomization**: The unit of random assignment, whether assignment was stratified, and any restrictions on treatment assignment probabilities are clear. Details specified by the definition of the named design count unless the paper describes a conflicting procedure.
4. **Outcome measurement:** Outcomes, coding, timing, and primary or secondary status are fully reported.
5. **Participant flow:** Numbers recruited, randomized, exposed, followed, and analyzed are reported as applicable.

### Statistical methods

6. **Estimand:** The causal or descriptive quantity being estimated is explicitly defined, whether presented as an estimand, a target parameter, a parameter of interest, or a well-defined causal effect.
7. **Estimator/model:** The statistical operation used to estimate the estimand is reconstructable from the text, table, or table notes.
8. **Analysis unit:** The reader can determine whether observations are participants, profiles, choices, sessions, or another unit.
9. **Coding and reference categories:** Treatment coding, outcome coding, omitted categories, and reference levels are explicit.
10. **Specification:** Covariates, fixed effects, weights, transformations, and column-to-column specification changes are explicit.
11. **Dependence and inference:** Standard errors, clustering, repeated-observation dependence, bootstrap or permutation procedures, and confidence-interval construction are explicit.
12. **Missingness and attrition:** Inclusion rules, missing outcomes, exclusions, attrition, and corresponding adjustments are explicit.
13. **Multiplicity and analysis status:** Multiple-testing procedures and prespecified versus exploratory analyses are distinguished.

### Results

14. **Analysis sample:** The number of observations used in each focal analysis is reported.
15. **Group quantities:** Relevant control means, treatment means, marginal means, or other raw quantities are reported.
16. **Effect and uncertainty:** Effect estimates and standard errors or confidence intervals are reported.
17. **Model-to-result traceability:** Each focal numerical result can be connected directly to a particular outcome, contrast, specification, sample, and inference procedure.
18. **Robustness analyses:** Alternative specifications and sensitivity analyses are explained sufficiently to understand what changed.

### Validity assessment

19. **Internal-validity threats:** Attrition, noncompliance, spillovers, demand effects, measurement problems, and other relevant threats are discussed.
20. **Inferential scope:** The paper distinguishes the randomized contrast from broader claims about mechanisms, populations, and settings.

## Component-level scoring

Treat each criterion as a compound item when it contains multiple required components.

Display the score and evidence for every component. Give the overall criterion a score of 1 only when every applicable component scores 1. Do not count component scores separately in the criterion totals.

For example:

- Criterion 1 components: target population, eligibility, recruitment, major exclusions
- Criterion 3 components: unit of random assignment, whether assignment was stratified, restrictions on treatment assignment probabilities
- Criterion 4 components: outcome definition, coding, timing, primary/secondary status
- Criterion 11 components: standard errors, clustering, repeated-observation handling, resampling procedures, confidence-interval construction
- Criterion 20 components: randomized contrast, mechanism scope, population scope, setting scope

Explain every component-level N/A judgment.

## Design-specific standards

### Ordinary treatment-control experiments

Award full statistical-model credit when the main-text regression table and notes jointly identify the outcome, treatment indicator, omitted control condition, analysis unit, adjustments, inference method, sample size, estimate, and uncertainty.

Do not require a redundant mathematical equation.

### List experiments

Require:

- Control list
- Treatment list
- Sensitive item
- Randomization mechanism
- Difference-in-means estimator
- Analysis unit
- Variance or confidence-interval procedure
- Sample size
- Numerical estimate

### Conjoint experiments

Award full credit only when the main article reports:

- Number of tasks and profiles per respondent
- Attribute levels and assignment probabilities
- Restrictions on profile construction
- Outcome coding
- Exact estimand
- Estimating model or computational procedure
- Analysis unit
- Reference categories
- Treatment of paired profiles and repeated observations
- Respondent-level clustering or another justified dependence adjustment
- Analysis sample size
- Direct mapping from the model to every focal AMCE, marginal mean, or related figure

The statement “we estimate AMCEs,” a citation to a standard conjoint article, or a pointer to an appendix is insufficient.

### Brief diagnostic randomizations

Score these separately. Do not average them with primary or formally analyzed experiments.

If only two percentages are reported without an explicit contrast, uncertainty calculation, or arm-specific sample sizes, score the missing statistical criteria 0.

## Additional checklist assessment

Complete this section only if an additional reporting checklist is supplied. Do not obtain one independently.

After completing the reconstructability assessment, provide a separate table for the supplied checklist.

For compound checklist items, divide the item into its required components. Give the item a score of 1 only if every applicable component is fully reported; otherwise score it 0.

Keep article-level items—such as title, funding, conflicts, registration, and data access—separate from experiment-level methods and results.

Do not use the overall checklist total as a measure of statistical-model clarity.

Report separately:

1. Overall completeness under the supplied checklist
2. Experimental-design reporting
3. Statistical-method transparency
4. Results transparency
5. Internal-validity discussion

## Required output

Produce:

1. An experiment inventory with one row per entry and separate **Study category** and **Experiment design** columns. List all design labels supported by the main article in full. Use **Unclear** if no design label can be determined and **N/A** for observational analyses.
2. A design map for every scored experiment
3. A binary criterion-by-experiment table
4. Separate totals for experimental design, statistical methods, results, and validity
5. A separate table for any additional supplied checklist
6. A concise explanation of every 0, identifying the exact missing information
7. A direct comparison of the papers’ statistical transparency
8. A consistency audit confirming that tables and table notes received the same evidentiary status as prose

Do not produce a combined article-level score that averages primary, supporting, and diagnostic experiments.

## HTML presentation and scoring evidence

Save the output as a polished, self-contained HTML file that opens offline.

The HTML must include:

- Embedded styling
- Clear navigation
- Desktop, mobile, and print-friendly layouts
- Full paper titles
- Experiment inventory with separate Study category and Experiment design columns, with all supported design labels shown in full
- Source-scope statement
- A prominent notice that AI-generated judgments await human review
- Experiment-level category subtotals
- A direct comparison table
- A consistency audit
- Downloadable scored JSON embedded in the HTML

For every core criterion and supplied checklist item, show:

- Identifier
- Complete wording
- Overall score
- Concise rationale
- Required components
- Component-level scores
- Supporting evidence or exact absence explanation

For each evidentiary record, provide:

- A concise verbatim anchor, subject to applicable quotation limits
- A page-specific paraphrase explaining the relevant evidence
- One-based PDF page number
- Printed page number, where available
- Table, figure, section, note, or footnote locator

Make every score in the criterion matrix link to its evidence details.

For missing information:

- State exactly what is absent
- Identify the main-article pages and displays reviewed
- Do not invent a quotation to prove an absence
- Do not treat an appendix pointer as evidence that the missing information was reported

For N/A judgments:

- Explain why the concept cannot logically apply
- Exclude the item from the denominator

Show numerators, applicable-item denominators, and N/A counts for every subtotal.

Keep core scores, supplied-checklist scores, article-level items, and experiment-level items clearly separated. Do not double-count component scores in item totals.

The downloadable JSON and visible HTML tables must be generated from the same scored records.

## Final constraints

Do not give credit for customary practice, inferred implementation, or information available only outside the main article.

Do give full credit when the main-text table and its notes together make an analysis completely reconstructable.

Apply the same standard to every paper and report the resulting differences without seeking a predetermined winner.

title: Parent coaching increases conversational turns and advances infant language development
source_scope: Only the supplied published main article was used: PDF pages 1–8 (printed pages 3484–3491), including main-text tables, figures, notes, and footnotes. No supplement, linked data, cited methods paper, or external source was consulted. The PDF ends with references on page 8 and contains no appended supplementary material.

experiments.name: Parent coaching intervention trial
experiments.classification_rationale: A single cohort of 79 families was randomized among PC, PC+, and no-coaching control. PC and PC+ were later collapsed for the focal intervention-versus-control analyses. Repeated follow-ups and manual diagnostics reuse that original assignment and therefore belong to this experiment.

title: Out-Competing Rivals: Armed Group Governance and Civilian Attitudes in Colombia
source_scope: Published main article only: PDF pages 1–14, including main-text tables, figures, notes, and footnotes. Supplementary material, preregistration, repository data, and external references were not consulted or credited.

experiments.name: Five-task paired-profile armed-group governance conjoint
experiments.classification_rationale: This is the article's central randomized study: 2,397 respondents each evaluated five pairs of hypothetical armed groups whose profile attributes were randomized. The same assignment supports forced-choice, rating, subgroup, and robustness analyses; those are not separate experiments.

direct_comparison.scope: One paper was assigned in this independent session, so cross-paper ranking is not possible. The table compares its separately scored experiments; cross-paper synthesis is reserved for the later validated-record stage.
direct_comparison.finding: E1 reports its ITT estimand and arm means clearly but leaves assignment probabilities, missingness, multiplicity, and resampling/CI construction incomplete. E2's Table 4 provides especially strong result traceability, yet exact letter text, assignment probabilities, bootstrap construction, multiplicity, and robustness remain incomplete.

consistency_audit.finding: Tables and notes received the same evidentiary status as prose.
examples: Table 3 note earned credit for inverse-probability weights, robust SEs, and two-sided testing.
Table 4 and its note earned credit for cell Ns, conditional/weighted/D-I-D estimates, block-aware randomization inference, one-tailed tests, 90% CIs, and 10,000 simulations.
Figure 1–2 notes earned credit for HC3 interval statements; their conflict with prose about bootstrapping was treated as ambiguity, not resolved by privileging prose.

consistency_audit.finding: Appendix pointers were not treated as evidence of omitted details.
examples: Appendix I did not supply ledger coding rules.

experiments.name: Third-party prediction experiment
experiments.classification_rationale: Additional experiment is identified, but no outcome is reported in the main article; all details are directed to an excluded appendix.

direct_comparison: This single-paper session does not make a cross-paper ranking. Within the article, Choice is markedly more statistically transparent than the supporting/diagnostic studies because Tables 2–4 and their notes identify models, coding, covariates, HC3 standard errors, and analysis Ns. NoChoice, Choice Stakes, IA, and diagnostics generally provide percentages and test statistics without fully reconstructable inference.

consistency_audit.finding: Tables and table/figure notes were given the same evidentiary status as prose. Choice received estimator/specification credit from Tables 2–4 and notes. Displays were not credited when they lacked a required component such as exact CI construction. Appendix pointers supplied no evidence.

title: Losing on the home front? Battlefield casualties, media, and public support for foreign interventions

reviewed_pages.boundary_note: All 17 PDF pages are the published main article. PDF page 17 ends with references, a Supporting Information availability notice, and the citation block; no supplement is embedded.

source_scope: Published main article only: PDF pages 1–17 (printed 1300–1316), including main-text tables, figures, notes, footnotes, references, and the Supporting Information availability notice. Linked Dataverse materials and online supporting information were not consulted and supplied no evidence.

additional_checklist.note: No additional reporting checklist was supplied; no separate checklist was scored.

experiments.name: 2020 U.S. casualty-information survey experiment
experiments.classification_rationale: A new U.S. sample received one base condition or one of two randomized information primes, followed by a formally analyzed withdrawal-support outcome. The authors call it a validation of their main quasi-experimental result, so it is supporting rather than the article's primary empirical design.

direct_comparison.scope: Single-paper independent assessment; cross-paper synthesis deferred.

rows.note: No randomized experiment was primary; the article's principal designs were quasi-experimental/observational.
One formally analyzed U.S. survey experiment.
The placebo reassignment of match dates is an inference procedure within O3, not a separately fielded randomization.

findings: Table 2 and its note received the same evidentiary status as prose: they earned credit for analysis unit, models, covariates, sample size, robust standard errors, coefficients, uncertainty, and robustness specifications.
The sole base condition plus the two treatment coefficient rows were accepted as identifying the omitted comparator; no redundant regression equation was required.

No credit was awarded for details absent from prose and displays, including exact scripts, casualty numbers, outcome category mapping, arm sizes, assignment probabilities, weighting status, and missing-data rules.
Pointers to the online appendix, Supporting Information, and Dataverse were recorded only as scope notices and never treated as substantive evidence.

direct_comparison.scope: Within-paper experiment comparison; only one paper was assigned in this independent session.
direct_comparison.finding: The three legislative experiments have the same core profile: explicit arm means and estimands but missing study-specific sample sizes, assignment probabilities, complete intervention texts, weighting construction, full models, and dependence/uncertainty procedures. The brief Supreme Court randomization is less transparent because it reports only a 15/18 directional tally. Cross-paper comparison is not possible until independent records for other papers are available.

consistency_audit.statement: Main-text prose, figures, table, notes, and footnotes were given equal evidentiary status. Figure points and notes earned group-quantity, graphical effect-estimate, and analysis-unit component credit where sufficient; Table 1's complete OLS details were used for the observational inventory entry. No credit was withheld merely because evidence appeared in a display. Conversely, figure test labels and SI pointers did not earn credit for omitted models, sample sizes, weighting construction, or dependence procedures.
display_checks: Figures 1–3 and notes: party/arm proportions, graphical treatment differences, bill labels, and absolute interaction t-ratios recorded.
Figures 4–5 and notes: arm proportions, graphical treatment differences, and joint F-test p-values recorded; missing model/SE details remained zeros.
Figure 6 and note: randomized-assignment follow-up retained within Study 2, not treated as a new experiment.
Table 1 and note: OLS, outcome, covariates, SEs, and N recognized for the observational moderation analysis only.
Footnote 6: Study 2 attention-screener exclusion recognized, while excluded SI details were not imported.

consistency_audit.statement: Prose, tables, table notes, footnotes, and the article-embedded appendix received equal evidentiary status. Table 5 and its note earned credit for estimator, specification, uncertainty, clustering, sample size, and model-to-result mapping where complete; no redundant equation was required. Pooled table evidence was not treated as wave-specific evidence. External appendix/replication pointers supplied no evidence.

consistency_audit.statement: Prose, tables, figures, table/figure notes, and footnotes were given equal evidentiary status. Figure notes supplied household clustering and interval types for Studies 1 and 2; Table 3 supplied Study 4 condition structure. Appendix pointers were not credited for omitted items, stimuli, scripts, samples, or robustness outputs.
examples: Figure 1 and Figure 4 notes were credited for household-clustered one-SE bars and 95% confidence intervals.
Table 3 was credited for the six Study 4 strategy levels and essay-task structure.
Online Appendix references were treated only as proof that the main article omits the referenced detail.

title: Serious games may improve physician heuristics in trauma triage

execution_record.submission:
Act as an independent reviewer of experimental reporting. Evaluate whether a competent applied researcher can reconstruct each experiment and its statistical analysis using only the published main article.

Do not evaluate novelty, substantive importance, journal prestige, or whether you agree with the conclusions. Do not seek a predetermined winner. Apply exactly the same evidentiary standard to every paper.

## Papers

Review the following published main articles:

EXP034: attached article.pdf. DOI: 10.1073/pnas.1805450115.

## Source restriction

Use only the published main article, including its main-text tables, figures, table notes, figure notes, and footnotes.

Do not consult online appendices, supplementary information, preregistrations, registries, replication files, code, or external methodological references. A reference to excluded material does not supply the omitted information.

Use the 20 core criteria below to define the assessment. If an additional reporting checklist is supplied, use it only to define its scoring items and components; it is not evidence about the papers. If no additional checklist is supplied, omit the separate checklist assessment.

Do not search for or substitute any external reporting standard or checklist. Online access is permitted only to obtain the identified published main articles. All paper-specific evidence must come from those main articles.

## Unit of evaluation

First identify every distinct randomized experiment.

Classify each as:

1. Primary experiment
2. Supporting experiment with a formal statistical analysis
3. Brief diagnostic randomization or robustness check
4. Pilot with no reported outcome
5. Observational analysis

Score categories 1–3 separately. List categories 4–5 without scoring them as experiments.

Do not combine all randomizations into a single article-level score. Report primary, supporting, and diagnostic experiments separately.

A follow-up using the original randomized assignment belongs to the original experiment. A new randomized sample or manipulation is a separate experiment.

Classify each experiment using all labels supported by the design described in the main article: completely randomized experiment, cluster-randomized experiment, factorial experiment, conjoint experiment, survey experiment, or list experiment. If the article provides too little information to classify it, mark it Unclear.

## Binary scoring

Use:

- **1 = fully meets the reporting standard**
- **0 = does not fully meet the reporting standard**
- **N/A = logically inapplicable**

Do not award partial credit. If a material component required by a criterion is missing, score the entire criterion 0.

Use N/A only when the concept cannot apply to the design. Failure to report information is 0, not N/A.

## Evidence rule

A regression equation is not required when a regression table and its notes jointly make the analysis completely unambiguous.

A regression table may earn full credit when it clearly identifies:

- Outcome
- Treatment or experimental contrast
- Treatment and control coding
- Omitted or reference category
- Analysis unit
- Estimator
- Covariates or fixed effects in each specification
- Standard-error procedure
- Clustering or other dependence adjustment
- Analysis sample size
- Effect estimate
- Uncertainty measure
- Correspondence between the table column and the result discussed in the text

Do not reduce a score merely because information appears in a table rather than prose.

Conversely, merely naming an estimator—such as OLS, AMCE, marginal means, conditional AMCE, or bootstrap—does not earn credit when the reader cannot reconstruct how it was implemented.

## Design map

Before scoring, create the following map for every scored experiment:

- Target population
- Eligibility criteria
- Recruitment procedure
- Field dates and setting
- Number recruited and analyzed
- Experimental arms or randomized attributes
- Unit of randomization
- Allocation probabilities and restrictions
- Exact treatment and comparator
- Outcome definitions and timing
- Estimand
- Estimator or statistical model
- Analysis unit
- Variable coding and reference categories
- Covariates and fixed effects
- Standard-error and inference procedure
- Handling of clustering or repeated observations
- Missing-data and attrition rules
- Effect estimates and uncertainty

Cite the page, table, figure, or footnote supporting every entry. Write “NR” when an element is not reported. Do not infer standard practice.

## Core reporting criteria

Score every experiment on the following criteria.

### Experimental design

1. **Population and recruitment:** Target population, eligibility, recruitment, and major exclusions are fully reported.
2. **Experimental conditions:** Treatment and comparator, or all randomized attributes and levels, are reported precisely enough to reproduce.
3. **Randomization**: The unit of random assignment, whether assignment was stratified, and any restrictions on treatment assignment probabilities are clear. Details specified by the definition of the named design count unless the paper describes a conflicting procedure.
4. **Outcome measurement:** Outcomes, coding, timing, and primary or secondary status are fully reported.
5. **Participant flow:** Numbers recruited, randomized, exposed, followed, and analyzed are reported as applicable.

### Statistical methods

6. **Estimand:** The causal or descriptive quantity being estimated is explicitly defined, whether presented as an estimand, a target parameter, a parameter of interest, or a well-defined causal effect.
7. **Estimator/model:** The statistical operation used to estimate the estimand is reconstructable from the text, table, or table notes.
8. **Analysis unit:** The reader can determine whether observations are participants, profiles, choices, sessions, or another unit.
9. **Coding and reference categories:** Treatment coding, outcome coding, omitted categories, and reference levels are explicit.
10. **Specification:** Covariates, fixed effects, weights, transformations, and column-to-column specification changes are explicit.
11. **Dependence and inference:** Standard errors, clustering, repeated-observation dependence, bootstrap or permutation procedures, and confidence-interval construction are explicit.
12. **Missingness and attrition:** Inclusion rules, missing outcomes, exclusions, attrition, and corresponding adjustments are explicit.
13. **Multiplicity and analysis status:** Multiple-testing procedures and prespecified versus exploratory analyses are distinguished.

### Results

14. **Analysis sample:** The number of observations used in each focal analysis is reported.
15. **Group quantities:** Relevant control means, treatment means, marginal means, or other raw quantities are reported.
16. **Effect and uncertainty:** Effect estimates and standard errors or confidence intervals are reported.
17. **Model-to-result traceability:** Each focal numerical result can be connected directly to a particular outcome, contrast, specification, sample, and inference procedure.
18. **Robustness analyses:** Alternative specifications and sensitivity analyses are explained sufficiently to understand what changed.

### Validity assessment

19. **Internal-validity threats:** Attrition, noncompliance, spillovers, demand effects, measurement problems, and other relevant threats are discussed.
20. **Inferential scope:** The paper distinguishes the randomized contrast from broader claims about mechanisms, populations, and settings.

## Component-level scoring

Treat each criterion as a compound item when it contains multiple required components.

Display the score and evidence for every component. Give the overall criterion a score of 1 only when every applicable component scores 1. Do not count component scores separately in the criterion totals.

For example:

- Criterion 1 components: target population, eligibility, recruitment, major exclusions
- Criterion 3 components: unit of random assignment, whether assignment was stratified, restrictions on treatment assignment probabilities
- Criterion 4 components: outcome definition, coding, timing, primary/secondary status
- Criterion 11 components: standard errors, clustering, repeated-observation handling, resampling procedures, confidence-interval construction
- Criterion 20 components: randomized contrast, mechanism scope, population scope, setting scope

Explain every component-level N/A judgment.

## Design-specific standards

### Ordinary treatment-control experiments

Award full statistical-model credit when the main-text regression table and notes jointly identify the outcome, treatment indicator, omitted control condition, analysis unit, adjustments, inference method, sample size, estimate, and uncertainty.

Do not require a redundant mathematical equation.

### List experiments

Require:

- Control list
- Treatment list
- Sensitive item
- Randomization mechanism
- Difference-in-means estimator
- Analysis unit
- Variance or confidence-interval procedure
- Sample size
- Numerical estimate

### Conjoint experiments

Award full credit only when the main article reports:

- Number of tasks and profiles per respondent
- Attribute levels and assignment probabilities
- Restrictions on profile construction
- Outcome coding
- Exact estimand
- Estimating model or computational procedure
- Analysis unit
- Reference categories
- Treatment of paired profiles and repeated observations
- Respondent-level clustering or another justified dependence adjustment
- Analysis sample size
- Direct mapping from the model to every focal AMCE, marginal mean, or related figure

The statement “we estimate AMCEs,” a citation to a standard conjoint article, or a pointer to an appendix is insufficient.

### Brief diagnostic randomizations

Score these separately. Do not average them with primary or formally analyzed experiments.

If only two percentages are reported without an explicit contrast, uncertainty calculation, or arm-specific sample sizes, score the missing statistical criteria 0.

## Additional checklist assessment

Complete this section only if an additional reporting checklist is supplied. Do not obtain one independently.

After completing the reconstructability assessment, provide a separate table for the supplied checklist.

For compound checklist items, divide the item into its required components. Give the item a score of 1 only if every applicable component is fully reported; otherwise score it 0.

Keep article-level items—such as title, funding, conflicts, registration, and data access—separate from experiment-level methods and results.

Do not use the overall checklist total as a measure of statistical-model clarity.

Report separately:

1. Overall completeness under the supplied checklist
2. Experimental-design reporting
3. Statistical-method transparency
4. Results transparency
5. Internal-validity discussion

## Required output

Produce:

1. An experiment inventory with one row per entry and separate **Study category** and **Experiment design** columns. List all design labels supported by the main article in full. Use **Unclear** if no design label can be determined and **N/A** for observational analyses.
2. A design map for every scored experiment
3. A binary criterion-by-experiment table
4. Separate totals for experimental design, statistical methods, results, and validity
5. A separate table for any additional supplied checklist
6. A concise explanation of every 0, identifying the exact missing information
7. A direct comparison of the papers’ statistical transparency
8. A consistency audit confirming that tables and table notes received the same evidentiary status as prose

Do not produce a combined article-level score that averages primary, supporting, and diagnostic experiments.

## HTML presentation and scoring evidence

Save the output as a polished, self-contained HTML file that opens offline.

The HTML must include:

- Embedded styling
- Clear navigation
- Desktop, mobile, and print-friendly layouts
- Full paper titles
- Experiment inventory with separate Study category and Experiment design columns, with all supported design labels shown in full
- Source-scope statement
- A prominent notice that AI-generated judgments await human review
- Experiment-level category subtotals
- A direct comparison table
- A consistency audit
- Downloadable scored JSON embedded in the HTML

For every core criterion and supplied checklist item, show:

- Identifier
- Complete wording
- Overall score
- Concise rationale
- Required components
- Component-level scores
- Supporting evidence or exact absence explanation

For each evidentiary record, provide:

- A concise verbatim anchor, subject to applicable quotation limits
- A page-specific paraphrase explaining the relevant evidence
- One-based PDF page number
- Printed page number, where available
- Table, figure, section, note, or footnote locator

Make every score in the criterion matrix link to its evidence details.

For missing information:

- State exactly what is absent
- Identify the main-article pages and displays reviewed
- Do not invent a quotation to prove an absence
- Do not treat an appendix pointer as evidence that the missing information was reported

For N/A judgments:

- Explain why the concept cannot logically apply
- Exclude the item from the denominator

Show numerators, applicable-item denominators, and N/A counts for every subtotal.

Keep core scores, supplied-checklist scores, article-level items, and experiment-level items clearly separated. Do not double-count component scores in item totals.

The downloadable JSON and visible HTML tables must be generated from the same scored records.

## Final constraints

Do not give credit for customary practice, inferred implementation, or information available only outside the main article.

Do give full credit when the main-text table and its notes together make an analysis completely reconstructable.

Apply the same standard to every paper and report the resulting differences without seeking a predetermined winner.

consistency_audit.statement: Tables, figures, table/figure notes, footnotes, and prose were given equal evidentiary status. Table 1 earned credit for group means and its stated two-tailed t-tests; Figures 4–8 earned effect/uncertainty credit from their plotted quantities and 95% CI notes. No credit was withheld merely because evidence appeared in a display. Conversely, pointers saying full coefficients, treatments, or checks were in SI/Dataverse did not supply omitted main-article information.
examples: Study 1 Table 1 note was used for N=1,009, 1–7 outcome coding, and two-tailed t-tests.
Study 2 Figure 4–8 notes were used for OLS labels and 95% confidence intervals.
Figure/footnote pointers to SI and Dataverse were treated as absence evidence, not as reported methods.

title: Maternal Depression, Women’s Empowerment, and Parental Investment: Evidence from a Randomized Controlled Trial
source_scope: Only the supplied published main article, including its embedded Appendix A on printed pp. 853–854, main-text tables/figures/notes/footnotes. Online appendices, manuals, cited prior reports, and external files were not used as evidence.

experiments.name: Thinking Healthy Program cluster-randomized trial and seven-year follow-up
experiments.classification_rationale: This is the article's causal centerpiece: 40 Union Councils were randomized 20/20 to CBT plus enhanced routine care or enhanced routine care, with outcomes through seven years. Later waves reuse the original assignment and therefore remain one experiment. The article does not establish whether assignment was unstratified, so 'completely randomized experiment' is not added as a separate label.

rows.assessment: Best reported of the three: assignment, follow-up flow, Table 2 comparisons, and Table 3 ITT results are relatively transparent; exact exposure counts, outcome coding, complete models, dependence handling, sample counts for spillovers, and effect uncertainty for every focal analysis remain unreconstructable.
The list design identifies the sensitive item and reports two prevalences, but omits the four control items, Ns, estimator, and variance/CI procedure.
The placebo lottery reports only winner count and activation percentages; no valid comparator definition, formal contrast, analysis denominator, or uncertainty is supplied.

consistency_audit.statement: Prose, tables, figures, table notes, figure notes, and footnotes were given equal evidentiary status. Table 3 earned credit for its omitted C group, robust SEs, N, and index construction; Tables 2 and 4 earned only what their notes state. Missing information was not inferred from convention, and online-appendix pointers were not credited.
examples: Table 3 notes support treatment coding, robust SEs, and N=1,130.
Table 2 notes support two-sided t-tests and definitions.
Table 4 notes support bootstrap SEs only for out-of-sample tests and explicitly defer model details; no credit was given for those omitted details.

direct_comparison.scope: Single-paper independent session; cross-paper synthesis follows later.
direct_comparison.finding: All five country experiments have identical main-article reporting structure and therefore identical criterion scores. The article is strongest on outcome definition, analysis-unit identification, plotted marginal quantities, and describing robustness dimensions; it is weakest on full conjoint construction, sample flow, exact estimand/model computation, missing-data rules, and uncertainty construction.

consistency_audit.statement: Prose, Table 1, Table 2, Figure 1, its note, and footnotes 1–5 were treated as equal main-article evidence. Full credit was awarded where displays resolved a component (for example, focal treatment texts, competence coding, marginal means, reference level, sample ranges). No credit was withheld merely because evidence appeared in a display. Conversely, Figure 1's visible but undefined error bars were not assumed to be a particular uncertainty measure, and pointers to supplementary/Dataverse material supplied no evidence.

consistency_audit.statement: Main-text prose, Table 1, its notes, Figs. 1–2, and the displayed equation received equal evidentiary status. Table 1 earned credit for adjusted group quantities, samples, effects, and uncertainty; it did not earn credit for omitted SE/test construction. Two table–prose conflicts were scored as traceability failures rather than privileging either source.

findings.detail: Table 1 and its note support criteria 10, 14, 15, and 16 to the same extent as prose.
Diary interactions: Table 1 χ²(2)=6.06, P=.048; Results prose χ²(2)=8.70, P=.013.
Diary interaction partners: Table 1 χ²(2)=11.23, P=.004; Results prose χ²(2)=11.47, P=.003.
Pointers to SI were treated as evidence of omission, not as supplied methodological detail.
